paragraphs.heading: Sparta and Lacedaemon
paragraphs.text: Sparta was a leading city-state, or polis, of ancient Greece, in the region of Laconia in the southeastern Peloponnese. In classical times the state itself was called Lacedaemon, while Sparta meant its capital, a cluster of villages in the valley of the Evrotas River. That river, the largest in Laconia, gave the town fresh water. Modern Sparta is a provincial town, home to the regional government of Laconia.

paragraphs.heading: A society built for war
paragraphs.text: Sparta's social system and constitution were unlike any other in Greece, and tradition credits them to Lycurgus, a lawgiver who may be partly legend. Its society was intensely military. The full citizens, called Spartiates, gave all their attention to military training and physical fitness, and the law even barred them from productive work. Below them were free non-citizens, the mothakes and perioikoi, and at the bottom the helots, enslaved locals owned by the state, who made up most of the population. People almost never moved between these ranks.

paragraphs.heading: Training, women and helots
paragraphs.text: Spartiate men went through a harsh training system called the agoge. Spartan phalanx units were widely thought to be among the best in battle, though that reputation owed as much to propaganda as to real skill. Free Spartiate women had somewhat more legal rights than women elsewhere in the ancient world. Helots, by contrast, were treated with exceptional harshness, and they rose in revolt again and again.

paragraphs.heading: Rise to power
paragraphs.text: In the 7th century BC Sparta became the foremost land military power in the Greek world. In the 6th century it founded the Peloponnesian League, through which it dominated most of the Peloponnese. When Persia invaded Greece for the second time, Sparta was accepted as the leading land force of the Greek alliance, which also included the growing sea power of Athens. Spartan troops were crucial at Thermopylae under Leonidas and at Plataea under Pausanias.

paragraphs.heading: Victory and decline
paragraphs.text: Sparta led its league against the Athenian Empire in the Peloponnesian War of 431 to 404 BC, and won after Lysander's naval victory at Aegospotami. A short spell of Spartan dominance followed, with armies under Agesilaus II campaigning in western Anatolia to protect the Ionian cities. Then in 371 BC Epaminondas defeated Sparta at Leuctra, opening a period of Theban dominance and freeing Messenia from Spartan rule. Losing the slave labour of that region sent Sparta into a decline as a military power from which it never recovered.

paragraphs.heading: Later history
paragraphs.text: Sparta tried several times to win back control of the Peloponnese, until the Achaean League annexed it in the early 2nd century BC. After Rome conquered Greece in 146 BC the city regained some self-rule, and in Roman times it drew tourists and became somewhat prosperous again. In 396 AD the Visigothic king Alaric sacked it, and over the following centuries it declined, with much of its population moving to nearby Mystras in the medieval period.

paragraphs.heading: An admired legend
paragraphs.text: Sparta fascinated people in its own day, and it fascinated the West again once classical learning was revived. Admiration for Sparta even has its own name: Laconophilia. The older name Lacedaemon appears in Homer and in the historians Herodotus and Thucydides, and Spartans were often called Lacedaemonians.
